sents.t: The next morning, a hurricane warning was issued for the whole coast.
The storm was expected to reach New Orleans in two days.
Our hotel lobby was full of worried people.
All flights for the next day were canceled.
“An evacuation hasn’t been ordered yet,” the hotel manager said, “but if I were you, I would leave today.”
Outside, shop windows were being covered with wooden boards.
The grocery stores were crowded, and the shelves of bottled water were already empty.
People seemed calm, but serious.
“We’ve done this many times,” a waiter told us.
“You learn to respect the storm.”
We rented a car and drove north with thousands of other people.
A drive that usually takes five hours took eleven.
Lily read the news aloud while I drove.
“Schools have been closed. People are told to stay away from the coast.”
That night, we stayed in a small motel in Mississippi.
On TV, we watched the hurricane hit the coast.
Trees were pulled out of the ground, and streets were flooded.
Two days later, we got a message from the cooking school: “We are all safe. The building was damaged, but it will be repaired.”
Lily cried with relief.
“When we get home, let’s do something to help,” she said.

comp.q: When was the storm expected to reach New Orleans?
comp.fa: انتظار می‌رفت توفان کی به نیواورلئان برسد؟

comp.q: What did the hotel manager advise?
Why were shop windows covered with boards?
o: because the shops were closing forever
to protect them from the storm
comp.fa: چرا ویترین مغازه‌ها را با تخته پوشاندند؟

comp.q: How long did the drive north take?
comp.fa: رانندگی به سمت شمال چقدر طول کشید؟

comp.q: What happened to the cooking school?
o: It was damaged, but it will be repaired.
comp.fa: چه بر سر آموزشگاه آشپزی آمد؟

comp.q: What does “relief” mean in “Lily cried with relief”?
o: a happy feeling when a worry ends
comp.fa: «relief» در جمله‌ی «Lily cried with relief» یعنی چه؟
